lead: Each closed contour on a map encloses an area at a known level. Treat the ground between two contours as a slice with those two areas as its faces, add the slices, and you have the volume of earth or water below any level. This is how the capacity of a reservoir is worked out before a dam is built, and how a capacity–elevation curve is drawn for its operation. Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic; it completes the uses of contours.
prereq: You need: contour interval and the uses of contour maps from Contours: characteristics, methods and uses.

blocks.text: The area inside each contour is measured on the map with a planimeter (mechanical or digital), by counting squares on a transparent grid, or from the coordinates of points along the line (the coordinate method of area computation). A map area is converted to ground area with the scale: at 1:s, 1 cm² of map is (s cm)² of ground. At 1:5000, 1 cm² = 5000² cm² = 2500 m² = 0.25 ha, where 1 hectare = 10 000 m².
Let A₁, A₂, …, A<sub>n</sub> be the areas of n successive contours at a contour interval h.

Trapezoidal (end-area) rule:  V = h [ (A₁ + A<sub>n</sub>)/2 + A₂ + A₃ + … + A<sub>n−1</sub> ]
Prismoidal rule (n odd):  V = (h/3) [ A₁ + A<sub>n</sub> + 4(A₂ + A₄ + …) + 2(A₃ + A₅ + …) ]
blocks.where: V in m³ when areas are in m² and h in m. The trapezoidal rule takes the area to change linearly with height in each slice. The prismoidal rule treats each pair of slices as a prismoid whose middle area is the contour between them; it needs an odd number of contours (an even number of slices). If the number is even, use it on all but the last slice and add that slice by the trapezoidal rule.

blocks.text: Below the lowest contour the basin narrows to its deepest point. That last bit is taken as a cone or pyramid: V₀ = A₁ × h₀ ÷ 3, where h₀ is the height of the lowest contour above the deepest point.

sections.h3: Reservoir capacity and the capacity curve

blocks.text: The capacity at a level is the total volume of water below it, measured from the deepest point, so it is the running sum of the slices from the bottom upward. Plotting capacity (and area) against elevation gives the capacity–elevation curve, which is read at any water level during operation. Water below the sill of the lowest outlet is dead storage: it cannot be released and is left for silt. The storage between the outlet sill and the full reservoir level (full supply level, FSL) is the live storage, the water that can be used.

examples.question: A reservoir site is contoured on a 1:5000 map at a 2 m interval. The planimeter areas inside the contours are: 100 m, 1.40 cm²; 102 m, 4.40; 104 m, 8.20; 106 m, 12.80; 108 m, 18.40; 110 m, 24.40; 112 m, 31.40 cm². The deepest point of the valley is at RL 99.2 m, the outlet sill is at 102.0 m and the full reservoir level is 110.0 m. Find the capacity at each contour, the dead and live storage, and compare the trapezoidal and prismoidal answers for the live storage.
steps: Bottom cone, 99.2 to 100 m: V₀ = 3500 × 0.8 ÷ 3 = 933 m³.
Dead storage = capacity at the sill (102 m) ≈ 15 430 m³. Live storage (trapezoidal) = 284 433 − 15 433 = 269 000 m³.
The two differ by 1000 m³, under 0.4 %; the prismoidal value is the better estimate for a basin that widens smoothly.
examples.answer: Capacity rises from 933 m³ at 100 m to 284 433 m³ at the full reservoir level of 110 m (and 423 933 m³ at 112 m). Dead storage ≈ 15 430 m³; live storage 269 000 m³ by the trapezoidal rule and 268 000 m³ by the prismoidal rule.

traps: Using the map area directly. 1.40 cm² on a 1:5000 map is 3500 m², not 1.40 m²; the scale is squared for areas.
Applying the prismoidal rule to an even number of contours. It needs an odd number; add a leftover slice by the trapezoidal rule.
Measuring capacity from the lowest contour. The volume below it (the bottom cone, 933 m³ here) belongs in the capacity.
Calling capacity at FSL the usable water. Usable (live) storage excludes the dead storage below the outlet sill.
Unit slips with hectares: 1 ha = 10 000 m², so 1 ha × 1 m = 10 000 m³.

quiz.q: Write the trapezoidal and prismoidal formulas for volume from contour areas.
quiz.a: V = h[(A₁ + A<sub>n</sub>)/2 + A₂ + … + A<sub>n−1</sub>]; V = (h/3)[A₁ + A<sub>n</sub> + 4(even-numbered areas) + 2(remaining odd-numbered areas)], n odd.

quiz.q: What are dead storage and live storage?
quiz.a: Dead storage is the water below the lowest outlet sill, which cannot be released. Live storage is the water between the outlet sill and the full reservoir level.

quiz.q: Two contours 2 m apart enclose 0.6 ha and 1.0 ha. Find the slice volume by the trapezoidal rule.
Three contours at 1 m interval enclose 400, 900 and 1600 m². Find the volume between the first and third by both rules.
Using the worked example, how much water is stored between RL 104 m and RL 108 m?
Silt raises the bed of the reservoir in the example by 1.5 m over 20 years. Which storage is lost first, and why does the capacity curve need re-surveying?
quiz.a: Silt settles in the deepest part first, so dead storage below 102 m (about 15 430 m³) is filled first, then live storage. The areas at the lower contours shrink, so the old capacity curve overstates the water at every level until a fresh survey redraws it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Today reservoir capacity comes from a digital elevation model of the basin, built from drone or LiDAR survey above water and an echo-sounder (bathymetric) survey below it, and GIS computes the area and volume at any level in seconds. Repeated bathymetric surveys measure sedimentation and update the operating curves. Search for reservoir sedimentation survey, area–capacity curve and bathymetric survey.

figure.caption: The capacity–elevation curve of the worked example. Read across from a water level to the curve and down to the capacity; the storage between the outlet sill and the full reservoir level is the live storage of 269 000 m³.
